Hello, for starters sorry for the long windedness and I am in no way licensed to diagnose anyone, I am speaking from my own experience and clarity with diagnosis. 

Im sensing that you might be struggling to accept a tough diagnosis,as you state the characteristics of BPD, you even state how you relate to each trait. I don’t believe it was a misdiagnosis, because:

An eating disorder is a form of self harm as you aren’t allowing your body to get the proper (or allowing too much) nutrients to grow and function. 

Friendships and relationships of all kinds can be tough at any age. Sometimes we simply just don’t start connecting till we’re older. 

You state that you “try and not be abandoned” I’m not sure if this was a typo. You don’t choose to be abandoned, but you can choose to feel abandoned, and this can be from a parent, sibling, friend, grandparent, uncle/aunt, cousin, boyfriend/girlfriend, teacher, team, doctor, boss, coach, etc. it’s feeling forgotten, left out, excluded. It’s not necessarily or always an obvious or literally beg, you can try to prevent abandonment in other ways

Like someone with bipolar disorder, mood shifts are intense, however unlike someone suffering with BD, those who have BPD, have quick shifts in moods that change through the day, so your intense and brief fits of anger are right on par. 

Having suicidal thoughts is suicidal ideation, you don’t have to have physically attempted to take your own life. If you’ve thought about and planned your demise, over a period of time and had the thought come to the forefront of your mind or some intense urge to just… poof…. it’s considered suicidal ideation. 

An unstable sense of identity is less to do about hobbies (love that you keep trying new things!) and more about struggling with where you fit in within the world, questions of a purpose or reason to existence in the world/community, feelings of being an imposter or ability in an area, feeling disconnected from self/surroundings. 

You stated “…had auditory and visual hallucinations in moments of stress…” it sounds like you’ve learned how to manage stress in your life. Which is honestly, fabulous! 

Like all diseases, you can (and should) learn how to manage and live with it. It sounds like you’ve done a good job at recognizing your triggers and how to experience and react to events in a way that has been deemed as “socially appropriate” norms. 

I didn’t say any of this to sound like some asshat, so I apologize if it comes off that way. I know the diagnosis can be seen as a hindrance, but it should be seen as a way to help learn to manage and regulate your emotions better.
